Nickle & Dime Rapid Rooter Air Pruning: The "4 inch rule", isn't.

Here we have a Kettle of Rapid Rooters.

In the last grow I experimented with root pruning at the seedling phase to help out with issues that I was experiencing with germinating directly in this kind of a hydroponic setup. The lessons are of course transferable.

These rooters are only about an inch to an inch and a quarter high. Normally a tap root is said to appreciate about 4 inches, which is apart from the "4 inch rule" having no basis in science, and rather equates to marketing for other seedling media that just aren't the equivalent of Rooters.

Here is the "misinformation":

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XnwyvXwsh9Y

Don't get me wrong, he's developed his own technique based on "rules of thumb" and a lack of scientific understanding, and is getting the right results. But his knowledge is less transferable.

Studies have determined that tap roots are unnecessary and more problematic than they're worth for practical gardening reasons. The first 12" of soil contains the bulk of the nutrients, and is where the bulk of the roots form. So the tap root is merely for providing an anchor that makes it difficult if not impossible to transplant.

As such, they've experimented with means of automatic root pruning, known as air pruning, with special types of pots. The weed industry has already adopted that with their own style of air pruning pots. However they have yet to adopt pruning of the tap root, which occurs naturally with clones.

In Hydroponics, the tap root is useless. It doesn't help anchor it or anything. In fact it does the opposite as the single root stretches almost clear through the media and into the water. As such, even small plants can barely hold themselves upright. Instead, with a trimmed tap root, lateral root growth is powerful promoted immediately, and you end up with them grown right into the media/clay pellets, providing a useful anchor.

What I will demonstrate here is that you do not need the first four inches. We do not care about all of the nutrients being in the first X inches of soil or anything like that.

The problem that I last experienced with germinating was similar to what I described happening in the DWC netpots above. The tap root grows by itself and doesn't begin to branch out laterally until several inches. Or an inch more than the Rooter is tall. It either grows immediately into media, or is apt to be damaged and broken off anyway.

Regardless, as it stretches seeking a footing, it lacks any at all, resulting in the seedling failing to push its way up through the rooter, as growth concentrates on a doomed tap root. You can pinch it off with your fingers, or cut it, or allow it to air prune, which should be less disease prone. Lateral root development will begin immediately, densely populating the area of the Rooter, which would otherwise have little more than a single thread through it. Vertical growth will be promoted, and the seedling will shoot right out with a nice healthy root base that is ready to be immediately submerged.

Upon harvest, you will find that same big root knuckle as shown in the above video. It doesn't require any babysitting or special watering techniques. Just the proper understanding to apply the lessons universally and idiotic rules of thumb, so prevalent in the growing industry, always operate in contrast of acquiring the necessary understanding.
